transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Northstar - Dedicated autoscaling oscillation incident review
Date: 2026-02-05
Time: 5:00pm - 5:47pm PT
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Rachel Kim, Sean Gallagher, Allison Grant, Owen Phillips
Northstar Payments: Maya Reynolds, Jon Park, Eli Santos

Conversation

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Cool. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is quick post-incident review on the Dedicated autoscaling oscillation that drove the latency spikes. We’ll keep it practical—what happened, what we changed, what you should monitor, and next steps. This is tied to SUP-1844 on our side.

[00:18] Maya Reynolds: Sounds good. Appreciate you all jumping on. Our main concern is we don’t want this pattern again during peak processing.

[00:26] Sean Gallagher: Totally. And just to set expectations: we’ll share a customer-safe recap. We’ll avoid internal on-call names and all that, but we’ll be explicit about the mitigation knobs we changed.

[00:39] Owen Phillips: I’ll also make sure SUP-1844 has the final notes. Some of the updates were in Slack during the bridge, but we’ll centralize.

[00:47] Rachel Kim: Great. Maya, do you want to start with what you observed from your side? Then we’ll walk the timeline.

[00:55] Maya Reynolds: Yeah. So starting around 10:12 Pacific yesterday, we saw p95 climb from like 350ms to 1.8 seconds for chat completions. p99 was… it was ugly, like 4 to 6 seconds. And it was not a total outage, it was like bursts every couple minutes.

[01:15] Eli Santos: And we saw a bunch of 200s still, so it wasn’t errors. It was just like the system was breathing.

[01:21] Jon Park: On our side, our app pods were stable. The request rate was spiky because we batch at the edge sometimes, but not like 10x. More like 1.5x swings.

[01:34] Sean Gallagher: That “breathing” description is actually consistent with what we saw. Let me share the rough timeline.

[01:40] Sean Gallagher: At ~10:10 PT we started seeing increased queue depth on your Dedicated pool, and at the same time autoscaler started adding replicas. Then within 2-3 minutes it scaled back down. Then it scaled up again. So you get this oscillation, and the thing that hurts you is the cold start + KV cache warmup + batcher rebalancing.

[02:03] Allison Grant: Right, and on the graphs it’s like a sawtooth. Replicas 6…8…6…9…6. And latency tracks it with about a minute lag.

[02:14] Maya Reynolds: That makes sense. Why would it scale down so fast if queue depth was still nonzero?

[02:22] Sean Gallagher: Great question. It wasn’t literally zero, but the policy was using a short lookback window and a fairly aggressive scale-in. So momentary dips caused it to decide “cool, we can scale in,” and then your next burst immediately pushed it back.

[02:39] Owen Phillips: Also there was a point where the target utilization threshold was a bit too tight. It was trying to hug a number, and with bursty traffic it’s like overcorrecting.

[02:48] Rachel Kim: To translate: the autoscaler was doing what it was configured to do, but the config wasn’t stable for your traffic pattern.

[02:57] Maya Reynolds: Got it. So what did you change during the incident?

[03:01] Sean Gallagher: Three main things, and I want to be very explicit.

[03:05] Sean Gallagher: One, we increased your minimum replicas on the Dedicated pool. You were at min=2, which is okay for steady traffic, but with your peaks and the model warmup it’s not enough. We raised it to min=6.

[03:21] Jon Park: Okay, so you’re essentially paying for 6 baseline now.

[03:24] Rachel Kim: Yes, and we can talk separately about cost tradeoffs, but stability-wise that’s the right move.

[03:31] Sean Gallagher: Two, we increased scale-down cooldown. It was effectively around ~2 minutes. We moved it to 15 minutes.

[03:41] Eli Santos: Fifteen minutes seems long.

[03:44] Sean Gallagher: It is longer than default, yes. But for GPU-backed inference, scale-in is the risky part. Scaling out is usually safe-ish; scaling in churns caches and can create head-of-line blocking while the batcher re-optimizes.

[03:58] Allison Grant: And you can think of it as “don’t remove capacity until you’re sure it’s truly idle.”

[04:06] Sean Gallagher: Three, we added dampening to scale-in decisions. Basically, it requires consecutive low-utilization intervals before we scale down. The exact internal phrasing is “scale-in stabilization window.”

[04:21] Maya Reynolds: And did that fully resolve it?

[04:25] Allison Grant: After those changes, the replica count stopped thrashing. Latency came down and stayed stable. There was still an elevated p99 for about 20 minutes as caches warmed back up, but no more sawtooth.

[04:39] Jon Park: We did see a smaller blip around 11:40.

[04:42] Sean Gallagher: Yes, that was correlated with your traffic burst plus a node-level drain event. Not a failure, just normal maintenance. But because you had min=6 at that point, it didn’t cascade.

[04:56] Rachel Kim: I want to acknowledge: during the incident, our comms cadence probably felt a bit uneven because we were juggling mitigation and trying to verify. We’re aligning internally on update cadence and templates. (We have a separate initiative running on that.)

[05:10] Maya Reynolds: The updates were fine. We mostly needed “are you seeing it, what’s next,” and we got that.

[05:17] Rachel Kim: Good.

[05:20] Maya Reynolds: So what are the long-term fixes beyond configuration? Because if it’s just knobs, we can live with that, but it feels like a class of issue.

[05:31] Sean Gallagher: Agreed. Two parts.

[05:34] Sean Gallagher: Part A is we’ll keep the tuned config for you. That’s the immediate prevention.

[05:40] Sean Gallagher: Part B is engineering guardrails. We’re tracking this as an engineering item—Dedicated autoscaling stability guardrail—so customers can’t end up with a config that’s mathematically unstable for GPU inference. Internally it’s ENG-4829.

[05:56] Allison Grant: Guardrails like minimum cooldown floors, scale-in step limits, maybe a “never drop more than X percent within Y minutes,” that kind of thing.

[06:08] Eli Santos: Could you also expose a metric that says “autoscaling is actively changing replicas” so we can correlate it ourselves?

[06:16] Allison Grant: Yes. Today you can infer it from replica count time series, but we can expose an explicit signal. We’ve been doing similar for routing fallback signals too.

[06:27] Sean Gallagher: For this specific issue, I’ll send you the dashboard panel set that shows replica churn, queue depth, and token throughput. You should be able to tell in 30 seconds whether it’s scaling churn or a model/runtime issue.

[06:43] Maya Reynolds: Great.

[06:45] Rachel Kim: Can we talk a bit about what you can change on your side? Not blaming, just knobs that reduce sensitivity.

[06:53] Jon Park: Sure.

[06:55] Rachel Kim: The two things we saw in the request logs were: (1) bursts in concurrency because of batching, and (2) a wider max_tokens spread during peaks.

[07:06] Eli Santos: We bumped max_tokens recently for a couple endpoints.

[07:09] Sean Gallagher: That’s fine, but it increases tail latency and it increases variance in compute per request, which makes autoscaling more reactive.

[07:18] Allison Grant: Even if average stays the same, variance drives queue oscillations.

[07:23] Maya Reynolds: We can cap max_tokens on the peak path. Or separate the longer prompts into a different queue.

[07:30] Rachel Kim: Exactly. A separate route or separate pool is an option. But let’s start with the minimal change: keep your current routing, but cap max_tokens for the interactive flow, and push long-form jobs to async.

[07:45] Jon Park: That’s doable.

[07:47] Rachel Kim: Back to the Dedicated config. Sean, can you summarize what we recommend as the “stable baseline” going forward?

[07:55] Sean Gallagher: Yep. For your pool:
- min replicas: 6 (maybe 8 depending on growth)
- scale-out can remain relatively responsive
- scale-in cooldown: 15 minutes
- scale-in stabilization: require multiple consecutive low-util windows
- target utilization: slightly lower than before to avoid running at the cliff

[08:20] Maya Reynolds: Can you quantify “slightly lower”?

[08:23] Sean Gallagher: We moved target GPU utilization from ~70% to ~60% for the autoscaling policy. That gives headroom.

[08:33] Jon Park: That’s a decent amount of headroom.

[08:35] Sean Gallagher: It is. But for latency-sensitive workloads, headroom is what buys you p99. If you want to run hotter, we can, but we should treat it as a tradeoff and we’ll likely need a different policy signal than just utilization.

[08:50] Allison Grant: Sometimes queue depth or request latency itself is a better scale signal than utilization.

[08:56] Eli Santos: Do you support scaling on latency?

[08:58] Sean Gallagher: Not directly in the self-serve knob set today, but SRE can tune with multiple signals. That’s part of what we want to standardize.

[09:10] Rachel Kim: For this review, the key is: we have a known stable config now, and we’ll test it.

[09:18] Maya Reynolds: About testing—what do you suggest? We can do synthetic load but it’s never perfect.

[09:24] Allison Grant: Two-step approach. First, a controlled load ramp in a 30-minute window where we gradually increase concurrency and keep token sizes representative. Second, watch the replica behavior. We want to see monotonic scale-out and very slow scale-in. No sawtooth.

[09:45] Jon Park: We can do that Tuesday morning.

[09:48] Rachel Kim: Let’s pencil Tuesday. Owen, can you coordinate scheduling and make sure the right folks are on standby?

[09:55] Owen Phillips: Yep, I’ll coordinate with SRE coverage and we’ll put it in the ticket.

[10:01] Maya Reynolds: One more thing: during the incident, our team wasn’t sure when to page you vs just open a ticket. We did both.

[10:09] Rachel Kim: That’s fair. For Dedicated, the rule of thumb: if you see sustained p95 degradation over, say, 10 minutes and you’re impacting production traffic, open SUP ticket and request a bridge. We’ll formalize the threshold language in our playbook, but practically—if your customers are feeling it, pull us in.

[10:28] Sean Gallagher: And when you do, include region, model, approximate QPS, and a couple request IDs. That’s the fastest path for us.

[10:38] Jon Park: We had request IDs but didn’t know which ones were useful.

[10:41] Sean Gallagher: Any 2-3 representative ones around the spike is fine.

[10:47] Allison Grant: If you can include a timestamp range plus request IDs, that’s perfect.

[10:53] Maya Reynolds: Okay.

[11:00] Rachel Kim: Switching gears—credits or SLA discussions. I know it came up internally. Are you asking for credits for this incident?

[11:09] Maya Reynolds: Not right now. We want stability. If it happens again, we’ll have that conversation.

[11:14] Rachel Kim: Understood.

[11:18] Sean Gallagher: Another detail: we also noticed the scale-down step was dropping by 2 replicas at a time. We changed it to drop by 1. That’s part of dampening.

[11:29] Eli Santos: That seems sensible.

[11:32] Jon Park: Was the oscillation triggered by any Redwood deploy?

[11:36] Sean Gallagher: No direct runtime deploy aligned with the start. There was a routine node recycle, but the primary trigger was policy + traffic. We’re double-checking release logs, but we don’t see a regression event.

[11:54] Allison Grant: The latency spike pattern matched replica churn more than it matched any backend error rate. Errors stayed basically flat.

[12:04] Maya Reynolds: So main root cause is “scale-in too aggressive + spiky load + cold cache.”

[12:09] Sean Gallagher: Yes, that’s the short version.

[12:12] Rachel Kim: Okay. I’ll pause. Questions we haven’t hit?

[12:16] Maya Reynolds: Just one. If we go into an even higher peak, will we see slow scale-out? Like, we don’t want to be underprovisioned.

[12:24] Sean Gallagher: Scale-out is still responsive. We did not slow that down. We only slowed scale-in. For peak, it should add capacity quickly. The only limiter is GPU provisioning time if we need new nodes, but for Dedicated you have reserved capacity. So it’s mostly just bringing up replicas.

[12:43] Jon Park: Okay.

[12:45] Allison Grant: We should also confirm your burst capacity settings. If you’re expecting occasional 2x peaks, we can reserve a bit of burst headroom.

[12:54] Maya Reynolds: Let’s discuss that offline. But yes, we probably need that.

[13:00] Rachel Kim: Great. We’ll follow up.

[13:04] (Cross talk)

[13:05] Owen Phillips: Sorry, quick note—some of this will end up in a known-issues article on our side (Dedicated autoscaling oscillation patterns). It’s not public customer-specific. It’s a general workaround doc.

[13:15] Maya Reynolds: That’s helpful for our on-call runbook.

[13:18] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[13:20] Rachel Kim: Let’s do a recap and next steps, and we’ll give you time back.

[13:25] Rachel Kim: 1) We’ve already applied mitigations: min replicas to 6, scale-down cooldown to 15 minutes, scale-in dampening, smaller scale-in steps, and utilization target adjustment.

[13:38] Rachel Kim: 2) Allison will send a dashboard link set so your team can quickly see if it’s replica churn.

[13:45] Rachel Kim: 3) Sean will send a customer-safe recap for your internal stakeholders.

[13:50] Rachel Kim: 4) Jon will share a 24-hour traffic and token distribution sample.

[13:55] Rachel Kim: 5) We’ll schedule a controlled load test Tuesday and monitor together.

[14:02] Rachel Kim: 6) Longer-term, we’re doing guardrails work (ENG-4829) so this class of config doesn’t happen.

[14:10] Maya Reynolds: Sounds good.

[14:12] Jon Park: Works for me.

[14:14] Eli Santos: Yep.

[14:16] Sean Gallagher: Thanks everyone.

[14:18] Allison Grant: Thank you.

[14:20] Owen Phillips: Thanks.

[14:22] Rachel Kim: Alright. We’ll follow up in SUP-1844 with the recap. Bye.

[14:27] Call ended.
